results.summary: This project implements a 16-bit RISC-V CPU with a memory management unit in Verilog. It uses an external RAM system for program and data storage, with separate buses for read data, address/data, and control signals. Testing requires that external RAM to be connected, as the CPU cannot run standalone. The design is noted as a CPU plus MMU, but the documentation is brief and gives few details beyond the pin names and the need for external RAM.

This design drives a 7-segment display to show the text PILIPINASLASALLE one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. It also has a manual mode where a 4-bit BCD input selects which character to display. It is based on a Wokwi project and requires an external 7-segment display. Silicon tests confirm it works in default mode, and a second tester verified both modes, noting that a slow clock is needed and the demoboard clock button is poorly debounced.

This is a test structure that captures data on both edges of a clock using pulse generators of varying widths, with outputs for each width and a normal flop. It is intended to explore DDR throughput and flop aperture using Analog Discovery 3 hardware. The documentation is minimal and self-deprecating, stating the design is probably bad. It is a process/timing experiment rather than a functional block.

This analog design implements a time-to-digital converter (TDC) with an 8-stage delay line to measure the phase difference between start and stop signals. It includes a variable delay line with fine (25 ps) and coarse (145 ps) steps to generate known phase differences for testing. The TDC achieves approximately 75 ps resolution in post-layout simulation. It requires external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi and level shifters to drive the analog and digital inputs; the design serves no practical purpose beyond testing the TDC circuit.

This Verilog design implements a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned numbers and outputs their 8-bit product. It uses a structural approach with full adders and AND gates, and is intended to be tested with switches for inputs and LEDs for outputs on the TinyTapeout demo board. The project appears to be a student lab exercise, with the description noting it is based on a previous lab. Testing involves setting switches and verifying the LED output matches the expected product.

This project is a 4-bit by 4-bit multiplier that outputs an 8-bit product, implemented in Verilog. It uses layers of full adders to compute partial products and then sums them. Testing is done via a provided Python script that sets inputs and compares the output. No external hardware is required. The documentation is sparse, without diagrams or detailed explanation beyond the basic algorithm.

This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit numbers (m and q) to produce an 8-bit product p. It uses partial products and full adders in a Ripple-carry addition scheme. The project is described as an educational exercise from ECE2204, and testing is done through a testbench with various input combinations. No external hardware is mentioned, and the documentation is relatively detailed including a block diagram.

This design is a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit binary numbers and produces an 8-bit product using AND gates and full adders. It is a combinational circuit with no external hardware requirements. Testing involves applying two 4-bit numbers to the inputs and verifying the 8-bit output. The documentation is brief but includes a diagram and a basic explanation of the multiplication process.

This project implements a 4x4 array multiplier in Verilog using a structural design with partial products and 4-bit adders. It takes two 4-bit inputs (m and q) and outputs an 8-bit product (p). The design includes internal wires for partial products and intermediate sums, and was tested with a provided Verilog testbench. No external hardware is required. The documentation describes the circuit structure and testing approach.
